newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Astronauts aboard crippled Mir face long wait.
newsitem.headline: Astronauts aboard crippled Mir face long wait.

text.p: The U.S. and Russian astronauts aboard Russia's Mir space station, crippled by the worst accident in its 11-year history, face a tense two-week wait for a relief ship.

Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev said on Thursday there were no plans to return the three crew to Earth aboard their Soyuz escape craft unless the air pressure in the station falls below about three quarters of the current norm.
Mission Control, near Moscow, said it faced a "five-point emergency" after Wednesday's collision between Mir and a Progress cargo craft. A "seven" means abandon ship.
Another Progress will be launched in 11 days, carrying supplies to repair the damage, Koptev said. It will take it two days to reach Mir but the crew's problems will still be far from over.
The collision smashed one of Mir's four solar panels, cutting electricity by 25 to 30 percent in the whole station and forcing the crew to halt experiments and physical exercise.
A spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces, which will launch the Progress, said Mir's low power would make the docking "very difficult".
NASA officials said Russian space authorities were considering spacewalks to restore some power, but added that any repair would be difficult.

Russian space officials said the crew were deciding on the best berth for U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, who had preferred to sleep in the Spektr module until the Progress freighter pierced a hole in it on Wednesday.
The spokesman said Foale had not yet chosen a place to spend the night. "The most comfortable place is on the ceiling. It is usually given to a woman cosmonaut when there is one," he said.
Cramped conditions on Mir are far from ideal at the best of times. Foale has described it as "a very dirty and grimy camping trip in an old car".
The spokesman said the crew, also including mission commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, had been urged to get a good night's sleep after a stressful day.

A committee including NASA officials and Mir's designer met for three hours to work out details of the repair mission. Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov told Reuters only Russian supplies, including specialised electric cables, were needed.
Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, who advises President Boris Yeltsin on space and aviation matters, visited Mission Control and was expected to report to the Kremlin leader.
The Soviet-built Mir, which means both "Peace" and "World" in Russian, is caught in a vicious circle.

The collision knocked its solar panels out of line with the Sun, reducing its power. And with low power the crew were finding it hard to realign the ungainly 140-tonne complex of interconnecting modules.

Mission Control spokesman Valery Latyshev said all the experiments were cancelled to save power and the crew would no longer take the oxygen-burning exercise they normally have to do to combat the effects of weightlessness on the body.

If the crew were forced to evacuate it would recall memories of the 1970 Apollo 13 mission, when three U.S. astronauts abandoned ship after an explosion. As the world held its breath, they defied long odds and made it home in a tiny lunar landing craft that was short on air, power and heating.
In Mir's case, however, the lifeboat is a state-of-the-art Soyuz TM-25, specifically designed for the return journey.
More of a headache back on Earth would be the fate of the massive Mir complex if it were abandoned. It is too big to burn up in the atmosphere and could fall on a built-up area.

The Russian space programme has come under fire from U.S. politicians concerned for the safety of NASA astronauts and about taxpayers' dollars pumped into the Mir programme as a test-bed for the planned international space station, Alpha.
Moscow and Washington have exchanged harsh words over delays in Russia's part of the project, due to be launched next year.
